job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here's a section-by-section review. I've grouped issues by section but numbered them continuously so staff can reference them easily.

**Sec. 2(1)(A) — Definition of "commercial deep seabed mining"**

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "by a single vessel."** The 10,000-ton threshold is measured per vessel, not per operator, project, or contract area, so a company can run several vessels each recovering 9,999 tons and never trigger the prohibition. This is the most obvious fleet-splitting loophole in the bill.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "per year" is undefined.** The bill does not say calendar year, fiscal year, or rolling 12-month period, so an operator could front-load recovery in December and January and lift nearly 20,000 tons in a few weeks while staying under the annual cap in each year.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "metric tons" with no wet/dry basis.** Polymetallic nodules can carry substantial water weight; without specifying wet or dry weight (or in-situ vs. processed), the threshold is contestable and operators will argue for whichever measure favors them.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "recovery" is undefined.** It is unclear whether recovery occurs at collection, when material is lifted to the surface, or when it is transferred to a transport barge; if a collector vessel transships to carriers at sea, each party can argue the other "recovered" the material.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — the 200-meter depth floor.** Recovery at or shallower than 200 meters is not covered at all, and the bill does not specify how depth is measured (seabed depth vs. depth of the deposit), leaving crust and sulfide deposits on shallower seamount flanks outside the prohibition.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "commercial" appears in the term but not in the definition.** The defined term implies a commercial purpose test, but the definition is purely volumetric, so there is a mismatch that litigants may exploit (arguing that non-commercial large-scale recovery is excluded, or that small-scale commercial recovery is).

**Sec. 2(1)(B) — Secretary's catch-all**

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — "the Secretary" is never defined.** No section identifies which Secretary (Commerce, State, Interior); the only Secretary named elsewhere is the Secretary of State in Sec. 6, which would be an odd reader of ecosystem risk. This alone could make the provision inoperable.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — "comparable" risk standard with no procedure.** The Secretary can expand the scope of a criminal offense by unstructured "determination" with no rulemaking, notice, findings, or judicial-review provision; this invites void-for-vagueness and nondelegation challenges, especially since Sec. 5(b) attaches a 10-year prison term.

9. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — no timing or publication rule.** The bill doesn't say when a determination takes effect or whether it must be published, so a company could face liability for conduct it had no notice was covered.

**Sec. 2(2) — Definition of "U.S. person"**

10. **Sec. 2(2) — entity list is far too narrow.** Only citizens and "corporations organized under the laws of a State" are covered, omitting LLCs, partnerships, trusts, lawful permanent residents, federally chartered corporations, and entities organized in D.C., territories, or tribal jurisdictions ("State" is undefined).

11. **Sec. 2(2) — no ownership or control test.** A Delaware parent can form a Marshall Islands or Singapore subsidiary to conduct mining with a foreign-flagged vessel and fall entirely outside Sec. 3(a); standard sanctions-style language ("owned or controlled by") is absent.

**Sec. 2(3) — Definition of "covered vessel"**

12. **Sec. 2(3) — 5,000-gross-ton floor.** Smaller collector vessels and modular systems escape the registry entirely, and the tonnage trigger has no relationship to the 10,000-ton extraction threshold in Sec. 2(1)(A).

13. **Sec. 2(3) — "equipped for the recovery" is ambiguous.** Modular mining equipment can be removed or kept aboard a separate support vessel, and the bill doesn't say whether a vessel that is capable of being equipped, or is equipped only part of the year, is covered.

**Sec. 3 — Prohibition**

14. **Sec. 3(a) — "engage in" covers only the act of mining.** Financing, insuring, contracting for, purchasing output from, processing, transporting, or providing technology to a foreign mining operation is not prohibited, so U.S. capital and offtake agreements can continue to underwrite the activity.

15. **Sec. 3(a) — "person in the United States" is unclear in scope.** It does not say whether the U.S. EEZ or outer continental shelf is "in the United States," nor whether a foreign national remotely operating equipment from a U.S. office is covered.

16. **Sec. 3(a) — "person" is undefined.** The Dictionary Act (1 U.S.C. § 1) will likely fill the gap, but the bill's own narrow "U.S. person" definition creates an interpretive tension about whether "person" is broader than "U.S. person."

17. **Sec. 3(b) — exploration licenses grandfather commercial recovery.** Exploration licenses (whether NOAA's under DSHMRA or ISA contracts) do not themselves authorize commercial recovery, yet the exemption lifts the prohibition for all "mining conducted under" them, effectively converting exploration rights into permanent recovery rights.

18. **Sec. 3(b) — "issued" by whom?** The clause doesn't limit the issuing authority, so licenses from any foreign government or the International Seabed Authority appear to qualify, and nothing prevents a rush to obtain licenses between now and enactment.

19. **Sec. 3(b) — no sunset, scale cap, or anti-transfer rule.** Grandfathered licenses can be renewed, expanded, assigned, or sold indefinitely, and the exemption applies regardless of tonnage.

20. **Sec. 3(b)/Sec. 8 — timing mismatch.** The grandfather cutoff is "enactment," but the Act doesn't take effect for 180 days, so the status of licenses issued during the 180-day gap is unclear.

21. **Sec. 3(c) — purpose-based exemption with no limits.** "For the purpose of environmental assessment" has no volume cap, duration, permitting requirement, data-sharing obligation, or restriction on selling recovered material, so large-scale test mining can be relabeled as assessment.

**Sec. 4 — Registry**

22. **Sec. 4(a) — no registration deadline or penalty.** The section does not say when registration is due, and Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register carries no consequence under this Act.

23. **Sec. 4(a) — no jurisdictional nexus.** The registry applies to "each covered vessel" worldwide with no U.S.-person or U.S.-flag limitation; NOAA cannot compel foreign operators, and the overbroad reach invites challenge.

24. **Sec. 4(b) — self-certified reports with no verification.** NOAA is given no inspection, audit, subpoena, or observer authority, and no penalty for false certification is attached in this Act (leaving only general false-statement law).

25. **Sec. 4(b) — reports don't collect what enforcement needs.** Reports must "describe" recovery activities but need not state tonnage, depth, location, or dates, so they will not establish whether the 10,000-ton threshold was crossed.

26. **Sec. 4 — no rulemaking authority or appropriation.** NOAA is given no express authority to issue implementing regulations and no funding, which weakens the program and invites challenges to any rules it does issue.

**Sec. 5 — Penalties**

27. **Sec. 5(a) — penalties begin at enactment, but the prohibition begins 180 days later (Sec. 8).** The civil penalty clause reaches "any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment," which is internally inconsistent and would be attacked as retroactive punishment for conduct that was not yet unlawful.

28. **Sec. 5(a) — "each day on which the violation occurs" sits awkwardly with an annual threshold.** It is unclear whether a violation occurs only on the day the 10,001st ton is recovered, on every day thereafter, or on every day of the year, which will drive litigation over penalty size.

29. **Sec. 5 — no enforcing agency, no injunctive relief, no forfeiture.** The bill does not say who assesses or collects civil penalties, provides no authority to seek injunctions or seize vessels or minerals, and creates no citizen-suit or whistleblower mechanism.

30. **Sec. 5(a) — "not more than $1,000,000" with no floor or inflation adjustment.** Penalties can be negotiated down to nominal amounts, and the cap erodes over a 10-year life.

31. **Sec. 5(b) — criminal liability stacked on a vague definition.** Willful violation of a standard the Secretary sets by "determination" (Sec. 2(1)(B)) is a strong rule-of-lenity and due-process defense, and corporate criminal liability for a 10-year offense may not survive challenge.

**Sec. 6 — International agreement**

32. **Sec. 6 — aspirational only.** "Seek to negotiate" imposes no obligation to conclude an agreement, no reporting to Congress, and no consequence for failure; it's unlikely to be enforceable or even reviewable.

**Sec. 7 — Duration**

33. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b) — direct conflict.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition continues until Congress finds by joint resolution that mining can be done safely; subsection (b) sunsets the entire Act after 10 years regardless. The sunset controls in practice, and companies can simply plan for year 11.

34. **Sec. 7(a) — no one is directed to produce the National Academies report.** The bill doesn't commission, fund, or set a deadline for the study, so the trigger for reconsideration may never materialize.

35. **Sec. 7(a) — "serious harm" is undefined.** There is no standard for the finding, and a joint resolution is just ordinary legislation anyway, so the provision adds little beyond what Congress can always do.

36. **Sec. 7(b) — sunset covers the whole Act, including enforcement.** Nothing preserves liability for violations committed before the sunset date or keeps the registry alive, so pending enforcement actions could be argued to lapse.

**Sec. 8 and general drafting**

37. **Sec. 8 — 180-day delay with no interim measures.** The gap gives operators time to ramp up recovery, stockpile, or obtain grandfathered licenses (see items 18 and 20), and it conflicts with Sec. 5(a).

38. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes Sec. 2(1)(B) or Sec. 5(a), there is no provision preserving the remainder.

39. **No relationship to existing law.** The bill neither amends nor repeals the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. § 1401 et seq.), so NOAA could in principle still issue commercial recovery permits under that statute while this Act purports to prohibit the activity.

40. **No definitions for "seabed," "mineral resources," or "exploration license."** Each is load-bearing in the prohibition or its exemptions and each is open to narrowing arguments (e.g., whether subsoil, crusts on hard substrate, or sediment-hosted minerals are "seabed" resources).

If it would help for the markup coverage, I can draft a short companion piece flagging which of these are most likely to draw amendments versus which are most likely to surface in litigation if the bill passes as written.
